label: GPT-6.1 Terra
output:
Jess texted me last night: “It’s one assignment. Don’t torch your job over it.”

She wasn’t being dismissive. We met student teaching at the same school back in 2012, and she knows exactly how much of myself I put into this job. She also knows what schools can be like when a parent is angry. She left teaching in 2019 and works in HR at a biotech in Cambridge now, which may have given her an even clearer view of the many creative ways a workplace can make your life difficult without technically firing you.

A few people in the group chat agreed with her. I understand why. I started typing out an answer and then realized I was about to send fifteen texts, so here we are.

For four years, my juniors in both sections of US History II at Cobb Street High have done an oral history project about busing and desegregation in Boston from 1974 to 1976. They interview someone in their family or neighborhood, make a ten-minute recording, and write a two-page reflection. Until now, I haven’t had a complaint.

This week, a parent emailed my principal, Dr. Halvorsen, and copied a school committee member. She said the project “reopens wounds” and “pressures kids to judge their grandparents.” Halvorsen wants me to quietly drop it. The three of us are meeting Thursday, November 19, at 3:15.

I’m not going to drop it. But I am going to change it.

The parent has a point. A student shouldn’t have to question a family member about a painful part of their life for a grade. Some families don’t talk about these years. Some kids may not have a relative who was here, or someone they feel comfortable asking, or anyone whose memories they can get to easily. And even when there is someone willing to talk, a teenager may feel caught between being a good student and being a good grandchild.

I don’t want to pretend that pressure isn’t real just because I like what the assignment has done in the past. My plan is to add an alternate option: students can interview a librarian or archivist, or work with recorded interviews from previous years, with permission. Nobody will have to interview their family.

But I want to keep the project because this is the history of the city these kids live in. The textbook gives it one paragraph. One paragraph for something that happened in neighborhoods they know, on streets they travel, involving people who might still be sitting across from them at a family dinner.

In 2023, D. interviewed his grandmother, who drove a school bus in Southie in 1974. She had never told anyone in the family about it. He played forty seconds of her recording for the class, and when it ended, nobody said a word for what felt like a full minute. I remember standing there wondering whether I should say something, and then realizing I didn’t need to. They were listening. They were letting it land.

Last year, one of my students found out her uncle had thrown rocks at a bus. She was upset, understandably. We talked after class twice. Her reflection was the best thing I read all year, not because she arrived at some neat conclusion about her uncle, but because she stayed with how complicated and painful the discovery was. I don’t think she owed me that experience, and I don’t think the quality of her writing makes being upset somehow good for her. I do think what she wrote mattered.

That’s the line I’m trying to find. I think students who are uncomfortable with this history often have the most to learn from looking at it. But I don’t get to force a kid to go home and have a conversation their family isn’t ready to have. Those are two things I believe at the same time. The assignment needs to make room for both.

And Jess, you’re not wrong about the risk. I’ve had tenure since 2021, but Halvorsen still controls my schedule and who gets AP. There are plenty of ways this could make next year harder. I’m scared about the meeting, honestly. Not in a noble, standing-up-for-what’s-right way. More in a waking-up-and-rehearsing-the-conversation-in-my-head way.

I’m also not looking to pick a fight with this parent. She raised something I needed to hear, and I want to listen to her on Thursday. I just don’t think the answer is to stop asking students to learn about what happened here.

I know you were looking out for me when you texted. I love you for that. You don’t have to agree with me; I just wanted you to know why I can’t quite call this “one assignment” and leave it there.

I’ll text you after the meeting Thursday.
